marble.name: Parallel and perpendicular lines
marble.subject: Mathematics
marble.description: Identify horizontal and vertical lines and pairs of perpendicular and parallel lines
marble.prompt: If you looks at a set of railway tracks or a window frame, can they point to which lines are parallel (never crossing) and which are perpendicular (meeting at a right angle)?

cluster.summary: Your child is exploring shapes and space — recognising circles, triangles, and squares, building with 3D shapes like cubes and spheres, and describing where things are using words like above, below, and beside.

misconceptions: Thinks parallel lines must be the same length
Thinks lines only count as parallel/perpendicular when they are horizontal or vertical; misses tilted pairs
representations: Real-world referents: horizon/table (horizontal), wall/lamppost (vertical), railway tracks (parallel), window corner / plus-sign (perpendicular)
The corner of a card or a set-square as a right-angle checker for perpendicular
A ruler slid between two lines, or the lines extended, to test 'always the same distance / never meet'
Letters and shapes marked up — an H has parallel verticals and a perpendicular cross-bar; a rectangle's sides
authoredAnswer: Yes — they are parallel. They stay exactly the same distance apart all the way along and would never meet, however far you extended them. Their tilt and their different lengths don't matter; parallel is about staying the same distance apart and never meeting.
probe: Show two genuinely parallel lines drawn tilted and of different lengths. Ask the child to PREDICT — 'if we keep extending both lines further and further, will they ever cross?' — and to say WHY before you do it. Then extend both lines to the edges of the page and OBSERVE that they never meet. Ask the child to EXPLAIN t

wrongAnswers.wrong: No — the two lines are different lengths
wrongAnswers.revealedBy: Answers 'no' and, on the reason tier, gives a length reason ('one's longer, so they can't be parallel')
wrongAnswers.fix: Show parallel pairs of very different lengths; define parallel by constant distance / never meeting, tested by extending — length is irrelevant (NCETM).

wrongAnswers.wrong: No — they are slanted, not straight across or straight up
wrongAnswers.revealedBy: Answers 'no' because the lines are 'slanted/wonky', or accepts only flat/upright pairs
wrongAnswers.fix: Rotate a known parallel pair off horizontal so the child sees the relationship is preserved; use tilted real examples (prototype/imposed-attribute: orientation wrongly treated as defining).

wrongAnswers.revealedBy: Calls a right-angle pair 'parallel', or points to a vertical line when asked for a horizontal one
wrongAnswers.fix: Re-anchor each word: parallel = run alongside, never meet; perpendicular = meet at a right angle; horizontal = flat like the horizon, vertical = upright. Rehearse naming while pointing.

before.name: Right Angles & Turns
before.reason: Perpendicular lines require understanding right angles
